D018-D002_h001.question:
It started about a year and a half ago, after the accident at the plant. Since then, I just haven’t been the same. Before that, I was pretty sharp at work—design reviews, calculations, keeping track of a dozen things at once were never an issue. But after the accident, my mind feels foggy. I misplace tools and drawings constantly, forget what I was about to do midway through a task, and my wife has to remind me about simple things I never used to miss. This only began after the accident, not when I was a kid or anything.

What really bothers me is how on edge I am. If someone comes up behind me at the shop floor or moves quickly into my field of vision, I practically jump out of my skin. Loud clanks or sudden movement make me brace like something bad is about to happen.

I also can’t shake this feeling that it’s my fault—that I should’ve double-checked the safety protocols, that if I’d noticed one more detail, nobody would’ve been hurt. I go over it in my head constantly, feeling guilty, like I failed them, and it’s drained any drive I had. Even simple projects feel pointless, and I struggle to even get started.

A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D002_h002.question:
It started about three years ago, after that big wildfire where two of my crew died. Since then, it’s like part of me is still up on that ridge.

Every so often, especially when I smell smoke or hear a loud crack in the woods, I’m not really in the present anymore. It’s like I’m back there—my heart pounds, I can see their faces, I hear the radio going dead. For a few seconds I honestly forget I’m just walking a trail; I feel like it’s happening all over again.

I jump out of my skin if someone taps me on the shoulder, even my grandson. Any sudden touch from behind and I whip around like I’m under attack. And I can’t seem to make up my mind about anything now—what to wear, what to cook, even which trail to patrol. I’ll stand there frozen, second-guessing myself.

I used to be sharp and organized, ran crews for decades, but my focus went downhill only after that fire. I lose track of what I’m doing mid-task. I keep thinking it’s my fault they died, that I should’ve called the evacuation sooner. I go over it every night, feeling guilty, and honestly, nothing I’ve done since seems to matter much to me anymore.
D018-D002_h002.options:
A. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    B. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    C. Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder
    D. Acute Stress Disorder

D018-D002_h023.question:
It started after what happened last spring. Before that, I mean, I was fine in school—could focus on lectures, study for hours, pull decent grades. Since then, my brain just… slips. I’ll be in a seminar and realize I’ve missed whole chunks because my mind wandered back to that night. Reading used to be easy; now I have to reread the same page over and over. This wasn’t an issue when I was a kid—teachers never complained or anything—only since the incident.

The nights are the worst. I keep having these intense dreams where I’m basically reliving parts of it. I wake up sweating, heart racing, sometimes I don’t even want to go back to sleep because I’m scared I’ll fall right back into it.

I also can’t shake this feeling that it was somehow my fault, like I should’ve done something different. Even when I manage to do well on an exam or a project, it doesn’t feel good. I don’t feel proud, just kind of empty or like I don’t deserve it.

And I get mad so fast now. Little things—someone bumping me in the hallway, group chat jokes—can set me off. I’ll snap at people and only realize afterward that I completely overreacted.
D018-D002_h023.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D018-D002_h024.question:
It started after that car accident about eight months ago. Before that, I was always pretty organized at work, could juggle my caseload, paperwork, all of it. Since the accident, my mind just blanks in the middle of sessions. I lose my place in treatment plans or forget what goal I was just working on with a child. It’s not like this has been a lifelong thing; it really began afterward.

When I hear tires screech or a horn blare, my heart just slams in my chest, my hands shake, and I feel like I’m back on that highway. Even something like watching a video with traffic noise in it during a telehealth session can set me off. I feel on edge almost all the time, like something terrible is about to happen, even when I’m just sitting at home with my husband.

What bothers me is that even when a kid makes real progress in therapy or I get positive feedback from parents, I can’t feel happy or proud. It’s like it barely registers. At home I snap at my husband over nothing—raise my voice, say really harsh things—and I hear myself, but I can’t seem to stop.
D018-D002_h024.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder

D018-D002_h025.question:
I’ve been working nights as a security guard for over 20 years. About a year and a half ago there was an armed robbery at the mall where I work. A kid got shot right in front of me. Since then, it’s like that scene is stuck on replay in my head. I’ll be walking the halls or even sitting at home and suddenly I’m right back there—hearing the gunshot, seeing the blood. I don’t try to think about it; it just slams into my mind.

I used to be proud of my job, you know, keeping people safe. Now I just feel like a failure, like I should’ve done more. Even when my supervisor praises me or my wife says she’s proud, it doesn’t land—I feel hollow, almost embarrassed, like I don’t deserve it.

My temper’s gotten worse too. I snap at coworkers and yell at my wife over little things. I’ll curse, blame them, then regret it later. Since that robbery, I also can’t focus like I used to—losing track on the cameras, rereading the same report. Before that night, my concentration was fine; this all started after the shooting.
D018-D002_h025.options:
A. Posttraumatic Stress Disorder
    B. Acute Stress Disorder
    C. Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (Predominantly Inattentive Presentation)
    D. Generalized Anxiety Disorder
